If a baby does not respond and is not breathing normally, call 911. Check for a brachial pulse for no more than 10 seconds. If there is no pulse, begin CPR on the infant. CPR should be performed with two fingers in the center of the chest, on the sternum, between the nipples for 30 compressions followed by two breaths. Repeat this process until EMS arrives, an AED becomes available, or advanced life support arrives.

title: What To Do in Choking? Steps to Manage Choking in an Infant (Below 1 Year) 1️⃣ Recognize the Signs Baby cannot cry, cough, or make sounds Difficulty breathing Lips or face turning bluish Weak or silent cough 2️⃣ Call for Help Ask someone to call emergency medical services immediately while you begin first aid. 3️⃣ Give 5 Back Blows (Most Important step) Place the baby face down on your forearm, supporting the head and neck. Keep the head lower than the chest. Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand. 4️⃣ Give 5 Chest Thrusts If the object does not come out, turn the baby face up while supporting the head. Place two fingers in the center of the chest (just below the nipple line). Give 5 quick chest thrusts about 4 cm (1.5 inches) deep. 5️⃣ Repeat Continue the cycle of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out or the baby starts breathing. 6️⃣ If the Baby Becomes Unconscious Place the baby on a firm surface. Start CPR and check the mouth for the object before giving breaths. ❌ What NOT to Do in Infant Choking 1️⃣Do not put your finger blindly in the baby’s mouth (blind finger sweep can push the object deeper). 2️⃣Do not perform abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) in infants under 1 year. 3️⃣Do not shake the baby to remove the object. 4️⃣Do not try to give water, milk, or food while the baby is choking. 5️⃣Do not delay calling for medical help if choking persists. transcript: How to perform immediate first aid when your child chokes on milk that parents must know. When a baby chokes on milk, many parents panic and quickly lift the baby up to pat them. This is a big mistake because the milk will flow into the baby's lungs, which is extremely dangerous. There is a risk that the baby will suffocate and stop breathing immediately. The correct approach is when you see your baby choking on milk or vomiting, quickly turn the baby on their side, cup your hand and pat the airway between the baby's shoulder blades to let the milk flow out of the mouth. If the baby does not cry, parents should flick the sole of the baby's foot to make them cry, which also helps stimulate breathing. If the baby still has difficulty breathing and turns blue, parents should quickly place the baby face down with the head slightly lower. Use the palm of your hand to firmly pat the baby's back to expel the milk from the respiratory tract. Once the milk flows out, parents should observe the baby's recovery signs. Choking on milk is a very dangerous accident that requires immediate and correct first aid on the spot. Parents, please be attentive and avoid making mistakes.

transcript: Most people know how to push the chest during CPR, but the breaths, that's where people mess up. Let me show you the right way to give rescue breaths to a child. Let's take a deeper look. When giving breaths to a child, tilt the head back, lift the chin, and plug the nose. Deliver two breaths breathing like you would normally breathe and letting them passively exhale. Seeing the chest rise visibly is how you know that your breaths are effective. With each breath, give just enough to see the chest rise. After you deliver the two breaths, continue with 30 chest compressions. A quick reminder to place the heel of one hand in the center of the chest and push hard and fast. Push down 30 times and continue the sequence of 30 compressions and two breaths until help arrives. When doing your compressions, make sure that you let the chest fully recoil in between each compression to give the heart enough time to fill back up with oxygenated blood. title: Infant Choking | Singapore Emergency Responder Academy, First Aid and CPR Training
description:
In some cases, infants might choke on foreign objects like food or small toys. It is important for the emergency responder to know what to do to clear the infant's airway.

1) Recognise signs by accessing airway. Some signs include loss of voice, increase breathing difficulty, and the infant's face turns blue.
2) Support the infant by using the sandwich maneuver
3) Support the head of the infant with your palm, and back of the infant's body on your forearm
4) Sandwich the infant with your other hand by supporting the infant's jaw with your thumb on one side, and the rest of your fingers on the other side
5) Place your forearm on the infant's chest
6) Straddle the infant faced down, with the head lower than the body
7) Use your knee as a support
8) Use the heel of your free hand to deliver 5 back blows between the infant's shoulder blades
9) Turn the infant from the back blow position 
10) Draw an imaginary line between the nipples with your ring finger
11) At the sternum, place your middle and index fingers next to your ring finger
12) Lift up your ring finger and deliver 5 chest thrusts over the lower half of the sternum using the same location and technique as chest compressions in CPR
13) If a foreign body is seen, remove the foreign body with your middle finger
14) Repeat the back blow and chest thrust technique until the foreign body is expelled or the infant becomes unconscious

title: Your Child is Choking, What do You Do? #firstaid. Performing the Heimlich maneuver on a child requires swift and precise action to dislodge an obstructed object from their airway. Follow these steps to administer the Heimlich maneuver on a child: Assess the Situation: Quickly evaluate if the child is genuinely choking. If the child is unable to cough, speak, or breathe, immediate intervention is necessary. Position Yourself: Stand or kneel behind the child, placing one leg between their legs for stability. Reach Around: With your arms, encircle the child's waist. Make a Fist: Form a fist with one hand, placing the thumb side against the child's abdomen, slightly above the navel and below the ribcage. Grasp with Other Hand: Grasp your fist with your other hand. Perform Abdominal Thrusts: Give quick, upward thrusts with both hands, aiming to force the obstructed object out. Continue Until Resolved: Repeat abdominal thrusts until the child can breathe, cough, the object is expelled or the patient loses consciousness. If they do lose consciousness then begin CPR Seek Medical Attention: Even if the child seems fine afterward, it's crucial to seek medical attention to ensure no internal injuries occurred during the maneuver. title: As babies learn to eat (specifically parents doing a baby-led weaning approach to solids) they will gag as they learn to chew and handle food while self-feeding.  🔴 Gagging is SAFE. Gagging is common. Intervening with gagging is NOT SAFE and can cause choking (trying to pull food out with your finger can lodge the food in the airway). You will see them thrust tongue forward with mouth open, bringing the food forward. 🔴 Coughing and sound is common with gagging - those are signs the airway is clear. Do not intervene.  Their face may appear red. It may take them several gags to move the food forward.  🔴 CHOKING is silent. They will be unable to make sound. They will turn blue. Take action right away with age appropriate interventions (back blows for infants 1 or younger, abdominal thrusts for > 2 year olds) 🔴 My biggest hurdle personally with BLW was learning to let my babies gag as they learn. Your main job is to offer safely prepared foods. Trust the learning process and enjoy solid introduction!  🔴 Research shows BLW shows no increased risk for choking if parents are educated and offering appropriately prepared foods. Purées will also cause gagging at first.  ➡️Mouth mapping is the natural process by which infants explore their world using their mouths. Through sucking, biting, and chewing, babies gather information about texture, shape, and temperature—basically, they’re building a sensory map of what feels safe and interesting to eat. Resistive food teethers are excellent for this skill! #babies #toddler #BLW #solids #babyledweaning

title: DON'T PANIC, ACT FAST! 🍼🚨 ​Choking on milk is every mother's worst nightmare, but knowing exactly what to do in those first 30 seconds can save your baby's life. 🛑 ​The Crucial Rule: If the baby is coughing or gagging—DO NOT intervene. The preferred method for infants under 1 is now a two-thumb encircling technique. This can help you achieve consistent, effective chest compression depth with less finger fatigue. First aid evolves as new research emerges, and these updates simply offer techniques that may help rescuers deliver even better-quality care. title: How to perform Child CPR with an AED
description:
If you see an infant or child collapse, CPR can save their life. Rescue breaths are especially important when performing CPR on a child in cardiac arrest. To give CPR to a child, call 911, push hard and fast in the center of the chest. After 30 compressions, give two rescue Repeat until help arrives.

If an AED is available, follow the prompts to provide a shock to try to restore a normal heart rhythm.

Be ready to save a life. Find a CPR class at https://www.heart.org/nation.
transcript: Products are shown for demonstration  purposes only. The American Heart Association does not endorse or recommend  any specific manufacturer or products. If you see an infant or child suddenly collapse  it is important to act fast. Helping to save a life is easier than you might think. Child CPR  is similar to adult CPR but it is especially important to give breaths to a child who  needs CPR. A child in cardiac arrest who is unresponsive and not breathing normally  will not survive without CPR. Your actions can help increase their chances of surviving  if you're alone. CPR on infants and children should always include breaths done in cycles of 30  compressions followed by two breaths. First check to make sure the scene is safe. If you're near  anything that can hurt you or the child move to a safe place. Next tap the child's shoulders and  shout are you OK. If the child is unresponsive shout for help. Point to someone and ask them to  call 911 and get an AED or call 911 yourself and put your phone on speaker mode so the operator  can help you. Now check for breathing scan the chest for 5 to 10 seconds looking for it to rise  and fall. If the child is not breathing normally immediately start CPR. With the child flat on  their back kneel beside them and lean directly over their chest. Place the heel of one hand or  two hands one on top of the other in the center of the chest. Then push hard and fast in the  center of the chest giving 30 compressions. It is important to keep a steady beat of 100 to 120  compressions per minute, which is about the same tempo as the song “Baby Shark” or the rate  of the music that you are hearing right now. Push down about 2 inches, about the height of  a credit card, letting the chest return to its normal position between compressions. Now after 30  compressions you'll give two breaths one after the other that makes the chest rise. Put one hand on  the forehead and the fingers of your other hand under the chin. Tilt the head back slightly and  lift the chin to open the airway. Pinch the nose, take a normal breath and cover the mouth with  your mouth, giving one breath for 1 second while watching for chest rise. Give another breath.  Don't stop compressions for more than 10 seconds to give breaths. Continue giving cycles of 30  compressions and two breaths until help arrives. [Music] Hopefully you never have to perform  CPR on a child. When possible use an AED - automated external defibrillator -  in your life-saving efforts. When the AED arrives use it immediately. Once the AED has  arrived place the child face-up on a firm, flat surface and follow the prompts of the AED.  Try not to interrupt compressions for more than 10 seconds. [Music] Turn the AED on and follow the prompts, which  will tell you everything you need to do. You must remove clothes and anything else that covers  the chest as AED pads must be placed directly on bare skin. If necessary wipe the chest dry.  Place pads on the chest. Use the smaller child pads if they are available. If child pads are not  available use the larger adult pads. Peel away the backing from the pads. Follow the pictures on  the pads attach them to the child's bare chest. Ensure there is nothing between the pad and the  child's bare skin. Plug the pads connected into the AED if necessary. Follow the prompts and let  the AED analyze the heart's rhythm. Make sure no one is touching the child and loudly state CLEAR.  The AED will analyze the heart rhythm. If the AED says that a shock is not needed, resume CPR. If  the AED advises a shock is needed make sure no one is touching the child and loudly state CLEAR.  Push the shock button to deliver the shock and immediately resume CPR with 30 chest compressions  and two breaths. Most AEDs will prompt you to analyze the rhythm again after about 2 minutes  of CPR. Keep doing cycles of 30 compression in two breaths and continue following the AED prompts  until the child begins to respond or help arrives. Hopefully you will never have to use CPR on a  child but know that CPR combined with using an AED provides the best chance of saving a life.  If possible use an AED every time you provide CPR. Again, if you see a child suddenly  collapse don't be afraid to start CPR. Your actions can help save a life.  To learn more visit heart.org/nation.

title: OLD 8b: Choking in Infants
description:
The second lesson in chapter 8 covers choking in infants. Infants are defined as 0 to 12 months in age. The administration of care for a choking infant is described, step-by-step. 

"If it’s a mild obstruction, stay with the infant and try to keep them calm. Do not do a blind finger sweep as you force the object further into the airway. Call EMS if they do not quickly rid the obstruction.

If it’s more severe, use back blows and chest trusts and call EMS. Begin BLS steps if the infant becomes unresponsive.  

Hold the infant in your lap.

Put the infant with their face down and their head lower than their chest; they should be resting on your forearm. Put your forearm on your thigh.

Support the infant’s head and neck with your hand and be sure to avoid putting pressure on their throat.

Using the heel of your free hand, deliver five back blows between the infant’s shoulder blades.

Using both hands and arms, turn the infant face up so they are now resting on your other arm; this arm should now be resting on your thigh.

Make sure that the infant’s head is lower than their chest.

Using fingers of your free hand, provide up to five quick downward chest thrusts over the lower half of the breastbone. Perform one thrust every second.

If the obstruction is not relieved, turn the infant face down on your other forearm and repeat the process.

Continue doing these steps until the infant begins to breathe or becomes unresponsive."

title: Chest Compression | Two-finger Technique | Pediatrics

Paediatric life support 👶🫀🚨 Following the rescue breaths, if there are no signs of life or if you are unsure:   - Start good quality chest compressions.  Rate: 100-120 min-1 for both infants and children.   Depth: depress the lower half of the sternum by at least one third of the anterior–posterior dimension of the chest (which is approximately 4 cm for an infant and 5 cm for a child).  - For all children, compress the lower half of the sternum:  - To avoid compressing the upper abdomen, locate the xiphisternum by finding the angle where the lowest ribs join the sternum (breastbone).  Compress the sternum one finger’s breadth above this.  - After each compression, release the pressure completely then repeat at a rate of 100–120 min-1.  Allow the chest to return to its resting position before starting the next compression.  - After 15 compressions, tilt the head, lift the chin, and give rescue breaths.  Continue compressions and breaths in a ratio of 15:2. Watch till the END for chest compression examples:  Continue resuscitation until:  the child shows signs of life (e.g., normal breathing, cough, movement) additional qualified help arrives you become exhausted. transcript: Products are shown for demonstration  purposes only. The American Heart Association does not endorse or recommend  any specific manufacturer or products. If you see an infant or child suddenly collapse  it is important to act fast. Helping to save a life is easier than you might think. Child CPR  is similar to adult CPR but it is especially important to give breaths to a child who  needs CPR. A child in cardiac arrest who is unresponsive and not breathing normally  will not survive without CPR. Your actions can help increase their chances of surviving  if you're alone. CPR on infants and children should always include breaths done in cycles of 30  compressions followed by two breaths. First check to make sure the scene is safe. If you're near  anything that can hurt you or the child move to a safe place. Next tap the child's shoulders and  shout are you OK. If the child is unresponsive shout for help. Point to someone and ask them to  call 911 and get an AED or call 911 yourself and put your phone on speaker mode so the operator  can help you. Now check for breathing scan the chest for 5 to 10 seconds looking for it to rise  and fall. If the child is not breathing normally immediately start CPR. With the child flat on  their back kneel beside them and lean directly over their chest. Place the heel of one hand or  two hands one on top of the other in the center of the chest. Then push hard and fast in the  center of the chest giving 30 compressions. It is important to keep a steady beat of 100 to 120  compressions per minute, which is about the same tempo as the song “Baby Shark” or the rate  of the music that you are hearing right now. Push down about 2 inches, about the height of  a credit card, letting the chest return to its normal position between compressions. Now after 30  compressions you'll give two breaths one after the other that makes the chest rise. Put one hand on  the forehead and the fingers of your other hand under the chin. Tilt the head back slightly and  lift the chin to open the airway. Pinch the nose, take a normal breath and cover the mouth with  your mouth, giving one breath for 1 second while watching for chest rise. Give another breath.  Don't stop compressions for more than 10 seconds to give breaths. Continue giving cycles of 30  compressions and two breaths until help arrives. [Music]

title: Help! Is Your Baby Choking on Milk – Here’s What to Know as a New Parent
description:
It can be alarming to see your baby cough, gag, or appear to choke while feeding. Whether you are breastfeeding or bottle feeding, occasional choking on milk is a common concern for many parents, especially during the first few months of life.

In most cases, what looks like choking is actually your baby’s protective reflex kicking in. Babies have immature swallowing coordination in the early weeks, and sometimes milk flows faster than they can manage. This can lead to coughing, sputtering, or milk coming out of the nose or mouth. While it can look scary, it is often harmless and resolves on its own.

That said, frequent choking or difficulty during feeding should not be ignored. It may be linked to issues like overactive letdown in breastfeeding, nipple flow being too fast in bottles, or even underlying conditions such as reflux or laryngomalacia. Identifying the cause can help you take the right steps to make feeding safer and more comfortable for your baby.

Here are a few things parents can watch for:

Coughing or gagging during feeds

Milk leaking from the nose

Difficulty breathing or turning red while feeding

Gasping or signs of distress after swallowing

If your baby regularly struggles with milk intake, seems to be in discomfort, or is not gaining weight as expected, it is best to consult a pediatrician or lactation consultant. They can help assess feeding technique, positioning, and feeding tools to prevent recurring episodes.

Always keep your baby upright during and after feeding, burp frequently, and never leave a feeding baby unattended. Recognizing the difference between normal reflexes and true choking is key to responding calmly and appropriately.

Your baby’s safety during feeding is a top priority. Being informed and prepared can make a world of difference in managing these common but stressful moments.

6: AED Steps for Children and Infants (2026)
description:
Chapter 6 discusses how to use an AED for children and infants. Along with provided a detailed definition of an AED, or automated external defibrillator, the steps for using an AED are explained. In the event the AED provides unexpected readings, such as “check electrodes”, those messages have been explained and appropriate steps are provided.

"An AED, or automated external defibrillator, is a device that recognizes ventricular fibrillation and other dysrhythmias and delivers an electric shock at the right time. The AED is nearly foolproof and will not allow you to make a mistake. It is safe for anyone to use.

Now, let’s review the AED steps.

First, retrieve an AED, open it, and turn it on.

Next, expose the person’s chest. If wet, dry the chest. Remove any medication patches.
Then, open the pediatric AED pads, peel off the backing, and check for a pacemaker or a defibrillator. 

Apply the pads. Apply one pad on the upper right chest above the breast.
For infants, apply on front of chest.
Apply the second pad on lower left chest below the armpit.
For infants, apply second pad to back.
Move away from the child.

Ensure that the wires are attached to the AED box.

Then, clear the individual, stop CPR, and instruct others not to touch the injured or the ill individual.

Let AED analyze the rhythm.

If the AED reads to “Check Electrodes,” then ensure that the electrodes are making good contact.

If AED message reads “Shock,” then: Press and hold flashing shock button until shock is delivered.

Resume CPR for two minutes starting with chest compressions. 

Repeat steps 1-10."

Visit http://onlinecprcertification.net and learn how you can save a life. Get CPR certified today.

Video transcript:
In this video we will be showing you the techniques and sequence of child CPR. 

Always make sure the scene is safe for you and the victim. Check for response by tapping the victims shoulder and shout "Are you OK?". If two rescuers are present then activate emergency response system and get or call for AED. If only one rescuer is present and there is no response, that is, if the victim isn't breathing or only gasping shout for help and start CPR. 

Check for carotid pulse for at least 5 seconds but no more than 10 seconds. If you do not feel the pulse or the pulse is less than 60 beats per minute and signs of poor perfusion then begin CPR immediately. Starting with chest compressions. Remember, start compressions within 10 seconds of recognition of cardiac arrest. 

Push hard and fast, at a rate of at least 100 compressions a minute. Count out loud "1, 2, 3,..." up to 30 compressions. After 30 compressions open the airway using the head tilt chin lift method. Give two breaths, deliver air over one second to make the victim's chest rise. Give one breath every 3-5 seconds at a rate of 12-20 breaths per minute. 

Try to limit interruptions in chest compressions to less than 10 seconds. Continue with 30 compressions followed by two ventilations for a ratio of 30:2. Until an advanced airway endotracheal tube, combitube, or laryngeal mask airway is placed. Once the advanced airway is placed then start continuous chest compressions with ventilations at a rate of one breath every 6-8 seconds for a rate of 8-10 ventilations per minute. 

AED with pediatric pads should be used as soon as it is available. Resume chest compressions immediately after the shock is given. Leave to activate emergency response system and get AED or defibrillator only if it has not been activated.

Remember for child CPR with one rescuer only chest compression to ventilation ratio is 30:2. Activate emergency response system and go for AED after 5 cycles or 2 minutes. For child CPR with two rescuers compression to ventilation ratio is 15:2. For two rescuers change the compressor every 5 cycles or 2 minutes to avoid fatigue.

title: How to do CPR on a Child who has a Trach Tube (Ages 1 to 12 Years)
description:
http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr
Cincinnati Children's Demonstrates Child CPR with Tracheostomy (Ages 1 to 12 Years).

Transcript:
You arrive on the scene: Check the scene for safety

Check the child for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder and shout. 

No Response

Call 911 immediately.  

If the child is lying on his stomach, turn him over onto his back. The child should be lying on a hard flat surface.

Check for Breathing and Signs of Life

Watch their chest for any normal movement.  Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. 

No Breathing or Signs of Life

Begin CPR:

1. Position the heel of one hand on the center of the child's chest; place your other hand on top.

2. With your elbows locked and straight, lean over the child’s chest and compress the chest 2 inches in depth 30 times. 

3. After the compressions, give breaths using a resuscitation bag attached to the trach.  Gently squeeze the bag and give 2 breaths – just enough to make the chest rise.

4. Continue with 30 compressions / 2 breaths, 30 compressions / 2 breaths, etc. 

If Breaths Do Not Make Chest Rise

a. Suction the trach tube. If the trach has an inner cannula, remove it and suction the length of the trach tube.

b. Change the trach if it is plugged or dislodged.

c. Give 2 breaths to the trach using a resuscitation bag.

Continue CPR until you see signs of life, another rescuer takes over, or help arrives.

For more information visit: http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr

In this video you will learn how to relieve choking on an adult and on a child. Use abdominal thrust to relieve chocking in a responsive victim one year of age or older.

Do not use abdominal thrust to relieve choking in infants. If you see someone clutching their throat with their thumb and fingers this is the universal sign for choking. You should ask them are you choking? If they cannot respond or simply nod yes, stand or kneel behind the victim and wrap your arms around the victims waist. Make a fist with one hand, place the thumb side of your fist against the victims abdomen in the mid-line slightly above the navel and well below the breast bone. Grasp your fist with your other hand and press your fist into the victims abdomen with a quick forceful upward thrust. 

Repeat thrusts until the object is expelled from the air way or the victim becomes unresponsive. Give each new thrust with a separate, distinct movement to relieve the obstruction.

description:
🚨 Did you know that knowing how to use an AED on children can save lives? 🚑💓

👶 When it comes to emergencies, it's crucial to be prepared. That's why today we're sharing a step-by-step guide on how to use an AED specifically for children. 👧🧒

1️⃣ First, make sure the scene is safe for you and the child.
2️⃣ Next, check for responsiveness. Gently tap the child and shout their name.
3️⃣ If they are unresponsive, call 911 immediately.
4️⃣ Locate the nearest AED and turn it on.
5️⃣ Attach the pediatric pads to the child's bare chest, following the instructions. Use the Front and Back Or Under Right Collarbone and Left Arm Pit. 
6️⃣ Once the pads are in place, the AED will analyze the child's heart rhythm.
7️⃣ If a shock is advised, make sure no one is touching the child and press the shock button.
8️⃣ Follow the AED's prompts for CPR until help arrives.

Remember, always stay calm and act quickly! 💪 Together, we can make a difference.

How to do CPR on a Child (Ages 1 to 12 Years)
description:
http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-children
Cincinnati Children's Demonstrates Child CPR (Ages 1 to 12 Years).

Transcript:
You Arrive on the Scene

Check the scene for safety.  Check the child for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder and shout.

No Response

Call 911 immediately.  

If the child is on his or her stomach, turn the child over onto his or her back. The child should be lying on a hard flat surface.

Check for Breathing and Signs of Life

Watch the chest for any normal movement.  Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. 

No Breathing or Signs of Life

Begin CPR

a. Position one hand on the center of the child's chest; place your other hand on top.

b. With your elbows locked and arms straight, lean over the child’s chest and compress the child's chest 2 inches in depth 30 times.

c. After the compressions, give breaths. Give breaths by tilting the head back, lifting the chin, and pinch the nose. Place your mouth over the child’s mouth and give two slow, gentle breaths – just enough to make the chest rise.

d. Continue with 30 compressions / two breathes, 30 compressions / two breathes, etc. 

Continue CPR until another rescuer takes over, you see signs of life or help arrives.

For more information visit: http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-children

title: CPR or basic life support is *ESSENTIAL* if your baby (under 1) or child (over 1 to 18 years old) stops breathing. The key is rescue breaths and chest compressions, here are the essential steps to follow from Mini First Aid 1. Check for danger - are they responsive? 2. Call 999 for help.  3. Open the airway and check for breathing for 10 seconds. 4. Give 5 rescue breaths. On a baby, place your mouth over their mouth and nose. On a child, pinch the nose and breathe into mouth. 5. Give 30 chest compressions. Placing 2 fingers in the centre of the chest for a baby and the heel of your hand for a child.  6. Press down to a third of the depth of the chest cavity. 7. Make sure they are on a hard surface. 8. description: Knowing the basics of CPR can help save a child’s life.
transcript: CPR is a life-saving action that can get oxygen and blood to the brain in an emergency. Getting trained in CPR is the best way to be prepared, but knowing the basics can help save a life. If a child doesn't seem to be breathing, shout and tap the shoulder and see if there's any response. Lay the child face up on a flat, firm surface. Kneel or stand to one side. You may be taught to check for breathing by seeing if the chest is moving, but don't spend more than 10 seconds doing this. Next, shout for help. Have someone call 911 and get an AED if possible while you start CPR. If you're alone and have a phone, call 911 and then begin CPR. Leave the phone on speaker. If you don't have a phone, do five rounds of CPR, then look for a way to call 911. Start with chest compressions. Put the heel of your hand in the center of the chest. For a small child, you'll use one hand. For a larger child, put your other hand on top with the fingers interlaced. Lock your elbows so that your arms are straight. Your shoulders should be in line with your hands. Push down fast and hard, about 2 inches deep. Let the chest come back up completely after each compression. Do this 30 times. Try to do about two compressions a second. After every 30 compressions, give two rescue breaths. To open the airway, tilt the head back and lift the chin. Pinch the nose closed. Blow into the mouth for about 1 second using just enough air to make the chest rise. After the chest rises and falls, give the second breath. If the chest doesn't rise, reposition the head and chin and try again. Keep doing compressions and rescue breaths until the child stirs or wakes up. Help comes and takes over. Or an AED says a shock is needed. To be better prepared for emergencies, sign up for a life-saving CPR training course from hospitals or other professional organizations.

title: CPR techniques vary by age. For infants (0-1 year): · Use two fingers for chest compressions if alone, or two thumbs with hands encircling the chest if with another rescuer. · Compress about 1.5 inches deep, 100–120 times per minute. · For breaths, cover the infant's nose and mouth with your mouth to make a seal. For children (1 year to puberty): · Use one or two hands for chest compressions. · Compress about 2 inches deep, 100–120 times per minute. · For breaths, tilt the head back, pinch the nose, and seal your mouth over theirs. For adults: · Use two hands for chest compressions. · Compress at least 2 inches deep, 100–120 times per minute. · For breaths, tilt the head back, pinch the nose, and give two breaths after every 30 compressions. In all cases: 1. Call emergency services immediately. 2. Start with compressions first (C-A-B sequence). 3. If unsure or untrained, do compression-only CPR—push hard and fast in the center of the chest and don’t stop. When the second rescuer arrives on the scene with the AED, turn on the AED and follow the prompts. 

"Apply pads to patient's bare chest."

"Plug in pads' connector next to flashing light."

"Apply pads. Plug in Connector."

"Analyzing heart rhythm. Do not touch the patient."

"Shock advised. Charging. Stay clear of patient. Deliver shock now."

"Press the orange--shock delivered."

"Pause. Begin CPR."

Rescuers' should continue CPR beginning with chest compression's and reanalyze ever two minutes. Two or more rescuers should change the compressor role approximately every two minutes to prevent compressor fatigue and deterioration in quality and rate of chest compression given. 

Rescuers' should try to change the compressor role in less than five seconds.  In special situations if there is water on the victim, wipe off the chest. If there is a transdermal medication patch remove the patch. If the victim has a lot of chest hair then shave with a razor and use new pads.  If the victim has implanted devices the pads must be at least one inch away from these devices. Do not place the pad directly over the device.

title: How to do CPR on an Adult (Ages 12 and Older)
description:
http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-adults 
Cincinnati Children's Demonstrates Adult CPR (Ages 12 and Older).

Transcript:
You Arrive on the Scene

Check the scene for safety. Check the victim for consciousness. Gently tap the shoulder and shout.

No Response

Call 911 immediately.

If the adult is on his or her stomach, turn the person over onto his or her back. The person should be lying on a hard flat surface.

Check for Breathing and Signs of Life

Watch the chest for any normal movement. Look for signs of life and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. 

No Breathing or Signs of Life

Begin CPR

a. Position the heel of one hand on the center of the adult’s chest.  Place your other hand on top.

b. With your elbows locked and arms straight, lean over the adult and compress the chest 2 inches in depth 30 times.

c. After 30 compressions, give breaths by tilting the head back, lifting the chin and pinching the nose. Give two slow and gentle breaths. The chest should rise with each breath.

d. Continue with 30 compressions / two breaths, 30 compressions / two breaths, etc. 

Continue CPR until another rescuer takes over, you see signs of life or help arrives.

For more information visit: http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org/cpr-adults

description:
If a baby is choking, they won’t be able to cry, cough or breathe. Here's what you need to do if a baby is choking...
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VIDEO TRANSCRIPT:

If a  baby is choking, they won’t be able to cry, cough or breathe. This is what to do if a baby is choking:
• Hold them face down on your thigh with their head downwards.
• Support their head with your hand.
• Hit them firmly on their back between their shoulder blades. These are called back blows. 
• Do this 5 times.
• Check if anything’s come out. If this has worked, the obstruction should have come out.
• If it hasn’t worked, turn the baby over so they are face up.
• Put two fingers in the middle of their chest – in line with their nipples.
• Push sharply down 5 times – this is called a chest thrust. The aim is to squeeze the air out of the baby’s lungs to dislodge the obstruction.
• Check their mouth to see if it’s worked.
• If it hasn’t worked call the emergency services.

While waiting for help to arrive keep repeating the cycle of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until help comes or the obstruction comes out. If the baby loses consciousness or become unresponsive at any stage, check their airway and give them CPR if they stop breathing.

title: Did you know that CPR for infants and children is different? One of the biggest differences is hand positioning for chest compressions. -Infants (under 1 year): Two fingers (thumbs)  in the center of the chest just below the nipple line called the encircling thumbs technique  -Children: One or two hands on the center of the chest depending on the child’s size. - the depth of the compressions is also different These small differences matter, and knowing the correct technique can make all the difference in an emergency. This is exactly why I teach hands-on Infant & Child CPR classes for parents and caregivers. Practicing the skills ahead of time helps you feel calm, confident, and prepared if you ever needed to use them. transcript: Ever wondered how CPR is different for a child? The process starts by checking if the child is responsive. If there's no movement and no normal breathing, you call for help immediately and begin CPR. Place two fingers in the center of the child's chest and push down about one third the depth of the chest using smooth, steady compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute. The force is firm enough to pump blood, but gentler than adult CPR. After 30 compressions, give two rescue breaths. Slightly tilt the head back, lift the chin and cover the child's mouth with yours. Give a soft breath, just enough to make the chest rise, not a full adult breath. Then go straight back to compressions. Continue cycles of 30 compressions and two breaths until help arrives or the child starts breathing on their own. That's how child CPR works. The same life saving technique adjusted with the right pressure and breath for a smaller, delicate body.

transcript: What to do if your baby is choking. I'm Dr. Yoshi, board certified pediatrician. I've gotten a ton of messages asking for a demonstration of what to do if your baby is choking, so here are the steps. First, recognize the signs. If a baby is choking, they might not be able to cry or cough. They might have difficulty breathing, and their skin might turn blue, especially around the lips and face. If you see these signs, act quickly but calmly. First, yell for help and have somebody call emergency services. If you are alone and have your phone accessible, call emergency services, put it on speaker, and quickly move to the next step. Next, for babies under one, support their head and their jaw with your hand. Place them on your forearm, facing down, and make sure that their head is below their chest. Make sure their head is still below their chest, and perform.

Abdominal thrusts and back blows can be life-saving when someone is choking and cannot breathe, speak, or cough effectively. title: How to Help a Choking Infant   #FirstAid #CPR
description:
Steps to take if your baby is choking

Things can happen very quickly in emergencies, so we’ve kept our descriptions clear and to the point.

Step 1: Verify that your baby is actually choking
Your baby may be coughing or gagging. This can sound and look scary, but if they’re making noise and able to take breaths, they’re likely not choking.

Choking is when a baby is unable to cry or cough. They also won’t be able to make any noise or breathe because their airway is completely obstructed.

Step 2: Call 911
Ideally, you can have a friend or family member call 911 or local emergency services while you take care of your baby.

Step 3: Place your baby face down on your forearm
Use your thigh for support. With the heel of your free hand, deliver five blows to the area between their shoulder blades. These blows should be both quick and strong to be effective.

This action creates vibrations and pressure in your baby’s airway that will hopefully force the object out.

Step 4: Turn baby over onto their back
Rest your baby on your thigh, keeping their head lower than their chest. With your index and middle fingers, find your baby’s breastbone (between and slightly below the nipples). Press down five times with enough pressure to press the chest down about one-third.

This action helps to push air from the lungs into the airway to potentially force the object out.

Step 5: Repeat
If the object still hasn’t dislodged, return to back blows following the same instructions above. Then repeat the chest thrusts. Again, tell the 911 operator immediately if your baby loses consciousness.

If the child does respond, then we can continue with abdominal thrusts. This is a bit small, but if you've ever heard of the Heimlich maneuver, under the chest line in an upward motion, attempting to dislodge the foreign object. If the child is not responsive, then we will continue with C P R. Quick side note, the Heimlich manoeuvre is not intended for mild airway obstruction. So if you can hear the child coughing or breathing, don't continue with that procedure. If the child is not responsive, then we'll continue with C P R. First, call to a friend if there's one around, and ask them to call 9 1 1 and grab an A E D. If available. If someone isn't around, you can call 9 1 1 after two minutes of the procedure that I'm about to show you. Alright, we're gonna check what's called the A B CS on the child. That's airway, breathing and circulation. First, the airway. Tilt the head back and open the jaw with the thumb. If you can see anything in the airway that might be easily accessible, feel free to try to grab It out. Then we'll check for breathing, see if you can feel any breath, see if you can hear any breath. And then circulation. We'll check the pulse. So the brachial artery that's at the bicep under the forearm, feel for a pulse there. If there's no pulse, or if the child remains unresponsive, we'll continue with C P R. And we're gonna start with chest compressions. So with the child, with the heel of one or both hands in the centre of the chest, between the nipples, we will go ahead. And we should be pressing down about one third of the depth of the child's chest. So press down and allow the chest to fully recoil, not a jerking motion. It should be rather smooth. description:
If a baby is choking, they won’t be able to cry, cough or breathe. Here's what you need to do if a baby is choking...

To find out how to help a baby who is choking, follow the steps in this video, or if you would like to view our Paediatric First Aid Refresher Training in full and try it for free, then get started with a free no obligation trial today! 
https://www.ihasco.co.uk/courses/detail/paediatric-first-aid-refresher-training

VIDEO TRANSCRIPT:

If a  baby is choking, they won’t be able to cry, cough or breathe. This is what to do if a baby is choking:
• Hold them face down on your thigh with their head downwards.
• Support their head with your hand.
• Hit them firmly on their back between their shoulder blades. These are called back blows. 
• Do this 5 times.
• Check if anything’s come out. If this has worked, the obstruction should have come out.
• If it hasn’t worked, turn the baby over so they are face up.
• Put two fingers in the middle of their chest – in line with their nipples.
• Push sharply down 5 times – this is called a chest thrust. The aim is to squeeze the air out of the baby’s lungs to dislodge the obstruction.
• Check their mouth to see if it’s worked.
• If it hasn’t worked call the emergency services.

While waiting for help to arrive keep repeating the cycle of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until help comes or the obstruction comes out. If the baby loses consciousness or become unresponsive at any stage, check their airway and give them CPR if they stop breathing.

description:
Learn how to recognize choking and perform the Heimlich maneuver on children in an emergency. This video provides essential information on identifying choking signs and demonstrates the critical steps to take to clear a child's airway safely. Stay informed and prepared to act quickly to save a life.

#LifeSaving #EmergencyResponse #Recovery #ApolloHospitals #TouchingLives #BeProHealth #heimlichmaneuver 


When an infant is choking, you can’t do a Heimlich maneuver on kids.
A couple of things that you should not do for children are:

Do not hold the child and start patting the back blindly.

Do not sweep the mouth with your finger without seeing the foreign body, because you can worsen the obstruction by pushing the object further inside.

If the child is choking — the child may turn blue, and there will be no sound coming from the mouth.

What you need to do is:

Hold the child securely and support the head with one hand.

Keep the head slightly lower than the body.

Using the heel of your other hand, give five firm back thrusts:
1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Then, turn the child over and look for any foreign body.
If visible, carefully remove it — but do not sweep blindly.

Now, using two fingers at the level of the chest, give five chest thrusts, pressing about 1 cm deep:
1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Continue alternating these steps until the foreign object comes out or medical help arrives.

Second, if you suspect your baby is choking, do not ever put your finger in their mouth and do a blind finger sweep to try to get the object out. Understand the characteristics of what makes them choking hazards. So round, hard, firm, rubbery, sticky, gummy. Those things are gonna be choking hazards that we want to complete, we avoid, or remove from the infant. Last, but certainly not least, is knowing how to respond if your baby is truly choking. You're going to calmly but very swiftly lower yourself and your child to the floor or a seated position. You're gonna support the baby's head. title: Infant and Child CPR: Why Smaller Hands Change Everything
description:
When a baby or toddler collapses, most people default to the adult CPR they learned years ago — and that's exactly the mistake that can cost a child their life. Infant and child chest compressions use different hand positions, different depths, and a different emergency-call sequence than adult CPR, because a baby's ribcage, heart position, and most common cause of collapse are all genuinely different from an adult's.

In this video we break down exactly how to perform CPR on an infant (the two-thumb encircling technique) and on a child past infancy (one- or two-hand compressions on the lower sternum), where the real dividing line between "infant" and "child" technique actually falls, why the 911-call sequence flips depending on whether you witnessed the collapse, how pediatric AED pads and dose attenuators work, and which five CPR myths are still getting repeated in living rooms and daycare break rooms every day.

title: Not all CPR techniques are the same—especially when it comes to infants. 👶 In this video, we break down three key approaches to infant CPR and when each may be used: 1. Two-Finger Technique — Single Rescuer    Ideal when you are performing CPR alone. This technique uses the pads of two fingers to deliver chest compressions at the center of the infant’s chest, just below the nipple line. 2. Two-Thumb Encircling Hands Technique — Two or More Rescuers    When a second rescuer is available, this technique allows the rescuer to encircle the infant’s chest with both hands and use their thumbs to deliver controlled chest compressions. It can provide better control of compression depth and reduce rescuer fatigue. 3. Heel of One Hand Technique    This technique may sometimes be considered depending on the infant’s size and physical development, although it is less commonly used for very small infants. So, which technique should you use? If you are the only rescuer, the two-finger technique is commonly used. When two or more rescuers are available, the two-thumb encircling hands technique may be preferred because it allows for more consistent and controlled compressions. In an emergency, knowing the correct technique can make all the difference. No parent or caregiver ever wants to be in a situation where they need to perform CPR on an infant. But knowing what to do in those critical seconds can mean the difference between life and death.

This step-by-step video guide will walk you through the latest, evidence-based techniques for performing CPR on an infant (under 1 year old). We demonstrate the entire process in a clear, calm, and easy-to-follow manner so you can feel prepared and confident.

Remember the key steps:

Check: Tap and shout. Check for breathing.

Call: Yell for help and call 108. Get an AED if available.

Compress: Push hard and fast in the center of the chest.

Clear Airway & Breath: Tilt the head, lift the chin, give 2 breaths.

Continue: Don't stop until help arrives or the baby shows signs of life.

title: What to do if a child is choking. 🎥 @doctor_yoshi  #motherly #lifesaving #safety #safetytips
transcript: How to respond if a child or adult is choking. I'm Doctor Yoshi, board certified pediatrician. First, recognize the signs of choking. Someone who is choking might be unable to talk, cough, or breathe, and they might be making the choking sign. Ask if they are choking. If they nod yes or you see the signs, act immediately. Shout for help and have someone call emergency services. If you are alone and have your phone accessible, call emergency services. Put it on speaker and quickly move to the next step. Next, for children 1 year and older and adults, stand or kneel behind them and wrap your arms around their waist. Make a fist with one hand, place it just above the belly button, and then grasp your fist with the other hand. Give quick upward thrusts. These are called abdominal thrusts or the Heimlich maneuver. Continue giving thrusts until the object is expelled or they can breathe, cough, or speak again. If they become unconscious, lay them on the ground and start CPR. Check the mouth for objects after each set of compressions. Continue CPR until they become responsive or emergency services arrive. Share this video to help spread awareness.

transcript: Your toddler can go from eating normally to choking in seconds. Here is your refresher. First, take a CPR and first aid course. Seriously. Watching a real here on Instagram is not the same thing. But if it's been a while, here is your refresher. If your child is coughing, forcefully, crying, talking, or making good sounds, their airway is still moving air. Don't immediately start pounding on them or sticking your fingers in their mouth. Encourage them to cough and just watch closely. Many kids will gag or cough the food back up on their own. But if they suddenly can't cough effectively, can't speak or cry, can't breathe, or are turning blue now you have a severe obstruction. Act right now. If multiple people are around, have somebody call 9 1 1 immediately. But realistically, with a complete airway obstruction, you cannot wait for emergency services to arrive. You need to act right away while help is on the way, as it will likely be too late and your child may die before they can get to you. Please do not blindly stick your finger into their mouth. If you can clearly see the food, of course try to remove it, but blindly sweeping around can push the object further back, making things much worse for a toddler or child over the age of one. Current guidance is five firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then five abdominal thrusts. For the abdominal thrust, put your fist just Above the belly button and below the breastbone. Then pull sharply inwards and upwards. Repeat 5 and 5 until the object comes out and the child becomes. Or the child becomes unresponsive. And yes, these need to be forceful. You are trying to create enough pressure to expel something out that is blocking their airway. A bruise or a broken bone is a much smaller problem than not being able to breathe. If they become unresponsive, start CPR, beginning with chest compressions, and follow your emergency training while 9 1 1 is on the way. And don't forget, prevention matters just as much. Toddlers should sit while eating. No running around the house with their food in their mouths. Be especially careful with small, round or firm foods like grapes, hot dogs, nuts, popcorn, raw carrots, and similar choking hazards. Cut grapes and hot dogs lengthwise into appropriate small pieces. title: HOW TO DO FIRST AID ON A CHOKING BABY USING BACK BLOWS AND CHEST THRUSTS
description:
Watch this first aid video and steps on how to help a choking baby under 1 year old 
A baby choking means that their airway is blocked or obstructed, commonly by food or objects such as small toys. Signs of choking in babies could be unable to breathe, cry, or cough and looking distressed. You want to act immediately before it becomes a respiratory arrest.

Step 1: Back blows 
 While holding the baby face down along your thigh with their head lower than their body, give five firm back blows between their shoulder blades.

Step 2: Chest thrusts
Turn the baby face up with their head lower than their body, and give five quick chest thrusts that are about 1.5 inches deep.

Repeat the steps until the food or object is dislodged from the airways, and check airway, breathing, circulation after every step. If baby is unresponsive, then commence cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

title: How To Save a Choking Baby
transcript: Imagine this. You are feeding your baby, and suddenly they go silent. It suddenly dawns on you that your baby can't breathe. Do you know what to do? Every second that your child can't breathe, oxygen is being cut off, brain damage, even death. And so here are five steps to take to save a choking infant's life. Step 1. First check is baby coughing loudly or breathing. If yes, don't interfere. Let them clear it. But if there is no breathing, or baby is struggling to breathe or turning blue, and shout for help and move quickly to step 2. To lay baby face down on your forearm, head lower than their chest, give up to five firm back blows between the shoulder blades. And if baby is still silently choking, move on to step 3. Turn them face up on your thigh again, head lower than body. Then use two fingers to give five quick chest thrusts just below the nipple line. Step 4. Alternate between 5 firm back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object comes flying out of baby's mouth or until help arrives. And if all this has been done and baby becomes unresponsive, call emergency services immediately and begin infant CPR to reverse. Every second counts in this scenario, and these 5 steps could be the difference between life and death. So please share this video with every parent that you know. Let's do better today.

title: POV: You’re Her Emergency Contact. Sources- Resuscitation Council Guidelines jslookbook on TT The thought of your baby choking is terrifying, but learning Infant Basic Life Support (BLS) is one of the most profound ways you can protect them. Because an infant's airway is incredibly narrow and their coughing reflex lacks the forceful power of an adult's, what might cause a brief coughing fit in an older child can easily become a deadly obstruction in a baby. When a baby's airway is completely blocked, irreversible brain damage from a lack of oxygen can begin in just four to six minutes. Paramedics often cannot arrive within that critical window, making your immediate intervention as a parent the true life-saving measure that keeps your child's brain oxygenated until professional help arrives. A crucial part of this training is learning to instantly recognize the difference between gagging, which is a normal, noisy reflex, and true choking, which is often completely silent. A baby who is truly choking cannot cough, cry, or breathe, and requires immediate, specific physical intervention. Because standard adult Heimlich maneuvers can cause severe internal injuries to a delicate infant, BLS teaches the precise, safe techniques of targeted back blows and gentle chest thrusts performed at a downward angle.  Mastering these specific mechanics replaces panic with empowerment, ensuring you have the confidence to act instantly when seconds count the most. #parenting #basiclifesupport #choking

title: A child choking is every parent’s worst nightmare - and I’m so grateful for @mikethesituation candor in sharing this moment, to help ALL parents.  A couple of quick things to note:  1. The @american_heart association does NOT recommend back blows for children/toddlers 1 and up (ie any child that can stand). They advise going straight to abdominal thrusts (what we used to refer to as “the Heimlich”). This can be confusing to parents, because other associations (such as the @americanredcross) DO recommend a combination of 5 back blows and then 5 abdominal thrusts. SO - SIMPLEST version: go straight to abdominal thrusts. If someone has medical training (and can tell when a child is still moving air) or training via the American Red Cross, they can do 5 back blows while the child is still moving some air (this is what I'd likely do on my own child). But, as soon as there's complete lack of air movement, switch to abdominal thrusts. 2. If you ARE doing back blows (ie in an infant or if you’re trained via the red cross), then this is not the way to do them. You need to use GRAVITY and FIRMNESS. (watch video while I explain).  3. No major medical group recommends using de-choking devices, including the AHA, Red Cross, ILCOR, and other international groups. While I won’t say DON’T buy it, if you’re a parent who wants to make sure you have EVERYTHING (I get it), I would absolutely say do NOT use it, do NOT waste time trying to find it, and do NOT even consider it, until you’ve done at least 2-3 cycles of REALLY GOOD choking first aid. Then, at most, attempt using one for 2-3 times, and if that doesn’t work, go back to first aid. title: Paediatric Life Support 🫀🚨👶 Following the rescue breaths, if there are no signs of life or if you are unsure:   - Start good quality chest compressions.  Rate: 100-120 min-1 for both infants and children.   Depth: depress the lower half of the sternum by at least one third of the anterior–posterior dimension of the chest (which is approximately 4 cm for an infant and 5 cm for a child).  - For all children, compress the lower half of the sternum:  - To avoid compressing the upper abdomen, locate the xiphisternum by finding the angle where the lowest ribs join the sternum (breastbone). title: Step by step guide you can trust in an emergency... 🚨 First: Confirm if the baby is choking. A choking infant (under 1 year) may: . Be unable to cry or cough . Make weak or silent sounds  . Show difficulty in breathing  . Turn blue or pale ❌ If the baby is coughing strongly or crying, do NOT interfere, let them try to clear it. 🚨If the infant is truly choking (Consciously) 1. Position the baby . Lay the baby face down along your forearm . Support the head and neck. (keep the head lower than chest) 2. Give five (5) back blows . Use the heel of your hand  . Deliver 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades 3. Turn baby over . Carefully flip the baby unto their back (still supporting head) 4. Give 5 chest thrusts . Place 2 fingers in the center of the chest ( just below nipple line) . Push down about 1.5 inches (4cm) . Do 5 quick thrust  🔁 Repeat  Keep alternating ➡ 5 back blows ➡ 5 chest thrusts Until .The object comes out  . The baby responds ⚠If the baby becomes unresponsive 1 Call for help immediately. . Call emergency services or ask someone nearby  2. Start CPR . Place baby on a firm surface . Begin chest compression ( 30 compressions)   . After compression open mouth and check if you will see object only remove if you see it clearly. ( Don't sweep blindly) .Attempt two rescue breaths  🔄 Continue CPR until help comes. title: Here is how you perform child cpr ages 1-12 years old. Check call care, then provide 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. title: Here's what you need to know👇🏼 Every parent's nightmare is their baby not breathing. Here's the thing: infant CPR is completely different from adults and children. The technique. The depth. The approach. And when your baby stops breathing, you can't use adult techniques. But here's what most people don't know: There are 3 critical steps that can save an infant's life, and knowing these could be the difference between bringing your baby back or losing them forever. Step #1: Start with Rescue Breaths Give 5 rescue breaths first. Cover both nose and mouth with your mouth. This gets oxygen into their system immediately. Step #2: Chest Compressions Are Different Place fingers around the back, use thumbs to compress. Compress just below the nipple line. Not your whole hand—just your thumbs. Press down one-third of chest depth. Give 15 compressions at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute. Step #3: The Ratio Matters Give 2 gentle breaths after every 15 compressions. Keep the cycle going: 15 compressions, 2 breaths. Continue until help arrives or they start breathing. --- The truth? Most parents don't know infant CPR is different, let alone how to do it properly. transcript: Hi, my name's Nick and welcome to this short lecture on CPR for pediatrics, which is a follow-on from the adult CPR lecture. Thankfully, it's a lot rarer for children to go into cardiac arrest than it is for adults. The guidelines for healthcare professionals who have a duty to respond in a pediatric emergency are slightly different to the adult guidelines with a bigger emphasis on ventilations. This reflects the fact that the more likely cause of a pediatric cardiac arrest will be asphyxia as opposed to a primary cardiac event in an adult. For the purpose of the guidelines, an infant is referred to as an under 1-year-old. The child is from 1 to 18, and an adult is over 18. Since we don't always have this information immediately to hand, if it looks like a baby, assume it's a baby. If it looks like a child, then it's a child. And if it looks like an adult, then it's an adult. The initial approach is the same as for an adult. Check for danger. Check for responsiveness, usually by pinching or flicking. Never shake an infant. Then shouting for help. The way we open the airway will vary a bit depending on the size of the child. In an infant, the airway should be opened with a head in the neutral position and a chin lift. As the child increases in age, a small degree of head tilt chin lift will be required, progressing further up to a full head tilt chin lift in adulthood. With the airway open, look, listen, and feel for normal breathing for no longer than 10 seconds. Infrequent noisy gasps can occur in cardiac arrest and are not a sign of normal breathing. Assuming someone has responded to your shout for help, get them to call the pediatric cardiac arrest team on 2222, stating clearly that it's a pediatric cardiac arrest and the ward location twice. Start by clearing the airway if necessary and attempting five rescue breaths. With an infant, use your mouth over their mouth and nose, and in a child, pinch their nose and use mouth-to-mouth. Remember that your lungs are a lot bigger than theirs, so give just enough volume to make their chest rise over a duration of 1 to 1 and 1/2 seconds. If the chest hasn't risen after five attempts, then move on. The airway may be blocked. After these five attempts, check for a pulse and other signs of life for no longer than 10 seconds. In an infant, use the brachial or femoral pulse, and in a child, use the carotid or femoral pulse. Assuming there's no pulse and no signs of life, or a pulse of less than 60 in a moribund apneic infant or child, then we can presume cardiac arrest. We perform 15 compressions to rate of 100 to 120 a minute. When compressing an infant or a child's chest, we aim to compress at least 1/3 of the depth of the chest. In an infant, we do it by using two fingers or two thumbs. In a child, use one or two hands to compress the chest depending on the size of you and the size of the child. Once the 15 compressions have been performed, then attempt another two breaths, and then continue CPR to ratio of 15 to 2. If you're ever on your own, perform 1 minute of CPR before going for help. Remember that in these circumstances, doing something is always better than doing nothing. I hope you never have to use these guidelines for real.

description:

Pediatric Cardioversion and Defibrillation (APLS):
An Automated External Defibrillator (AED) can be used on children and infants if indicated. 
Pediatric pads should be used if the child is less than eight years old or less than 25 kilograms. 
Adult pads can be used for children eight years and older.
Standard adult pads may be used for children if pediatric pads are not available. 
Some AEDs have a switch that can be set to deliver a pediatric shock. 
If available, turn the switch on when using on children younger than eight years old. 
If the AED cannot deliver a pediatric shock, an adult shock should be given.
For infants less than 1 year old, a manual defibrillator should be used if available. 
If a manual defibrillator is not available, an AED may be used. 
For synchronized cardioversion, begin with an electrical dose of 0.5 to 1 J/kg of the child's body weight. If ineffective, increase the energy level to 2 J/kg. For defibrillation (cardiac arrest with a shockable rhythm), first shock should be given at 2 J/kg and the second shock should be given at 4 J/kg.

title: CPR Lifeline AHA Infant BLS Rescue Breathing with VAM
description:
Respiratory support can be lifesaving for infants when they are not breathing adequately. In this tutorial, we demonstrate infant breathing using a bag-valve mask (BVM) under AHA BLS guidelines, leveraging the RQI HeartCode Complete platform and a Voice-Activated Manikin (VAM). You’ll see how to apply the correct technique, maintain a good mask seal, and respond to feedback in real time.
This video is ideal for healthcare providers, pediatric staff, neonatal teams, instructors, and anyone tasked with maintaining high-quality infant resuscitation skills. By combining visual demonstration with dynamic feedback, learners can internalize effective technique and confidence.
________________________________________
🔍 What You’ll See
• Setup of the RQI + VAM system for infant mode
• Proper head positioning (neutral / slight sniffing position) or technique for infants
• Mask placement over both nose and mouth with secure sealing
• Gentle ventilation and observing for visible chest rise
• Recognizing and managing leaks or imperfect technique as prompted by VAM
• Adjustments in airflow, mask seal, or positioning mid-practice
• How VAM prompts corrections to help you refine your technique
• Best practices & troubleshooting common errors
________________________________________
✅ Why This Matters for Your Training & Clients
• Feedback loop: The VAM’s real-time voice cues help learners self-correct, improving retention
• Visual + tactile learning: Videos strengthen muscle memory before in-person practice
• Demonstrates your training sophistication: Show prospective clients you use advanced simulation tools
• Higher standard training: Helps learners maintain skill proficiency between formal courses
• Confidence building: Seeing correct technique in action reduces hesitation during real events
________________________________________
📝 Clinical Notes & Guidelines
• Infant rescue breathing / ventilation: when an infant has a pulse but inadequate or absent breathing, deliver gentle breaths at around 1 breath every 2–3 seconds (i.e. ~20–30 breaths/min)
• Ventilation volume must be modest—just enough to see chest rise
• A proper mask seal over both nose and mouth is critical (infants breathe through both)
• Watch for excessive pressure or volume that could lead to gastric inflation
• If chest rise is inadequate, reposition airway, re-seal mask, or reassess technique
• Real-time feedback significantly enhances error correction and performance consistency

title: If you ever catch your baby putting something in their mouth that could cause choking, what you do next matters. If you can see the object, you can carefully remove it. 🚫 If you can’t see it, never do a blind finger sweep — that can push it deeper. 😮‍💨 If your baby is coughing, gagging, or making sounds that means air is still moving. 🚨 If your baby can’t cry, cough, or breathe: Call 911, then start infant choking first aid: ➡️ 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades ➡️ Flip, then 5 chest thrusts Repeat until the object comes out or help arrives. Even if they seem fine afterward, always have them checked by a medical professional. Make sure to keep small objects, coins, and food pieces out of reach. And make sure you, and anyone who cares for your baby, take an infant CPR & choking class. Preparation saves lives. 💛

title: SHARE with any parent or caregiver  This is one of the most terrifying moments for any parent. This mom saved her baby—and here’s what she did really well: She recognized choking immediately (a silent baby who isn’t crying, coughing, or breathing) She positioned the baby face down She delivered firm, effective back blows Here’s a clear, quick reminder of what to do: 	1.	Call 911 or shout for someone else to call 	2.	Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades 	3.	If still choking, give up to 5 chest thrusts using two fingers in the center of the chest 	4.	Repeat back blows and chest thrusts until the object comes out or help arrives 	5.	If the baby becomes unresponsive, start CPR immediately In a moment like this, panic is completely normal. You don’t need to be perfect—you just need to act. A few things that matter: • Don’t put your fingers in their mouth unless you can clearly see and remove the object • Don’t delay waiting to “see if it passes” • Stay focused and keep going until help arrives Knowing what to do ahead of time can make all the difference. title: How to Help a Choking Child or Adult (Everyone Must Know!)
description:
How to Help a Choking Victim. You never know what might happen and when you might need to know how to save someone who's choking. It's important that you learn how to find out if someone's is really choking next to you and how to help people in trouble. You'll have to know how to perform the Heimlich maneuver and there are special rules for how to save a choking child or choking dog. 

Music: https://www.youtube.com/audiolibrary/music

TIMESTAMPS
Assess the situation 0:33
Encourage them to cough 1:13
If the person can’t cough, slap their back 1:55
If the person can’t breathe, perform the Heimlich maneuver 2:46
Helping an unconscious person 3:39
Helping yourself 4:22
Helping pregnant women and obese people 5:24
Saving a choking infant 5:58
Saving a choking child 6:38
Saving an unconscious child 7:11
Saving a choking dog 8:03

SUMMARY
-Determine if the airway obstruction is partial or total to figure out what you should do to help.
-Coughing is the most effective way to clear the airways and push the stuck piece of food out of the trachea.
-Deliver up to 5 strong blows between the shoulder blades using the heel of your hand.
-Perform the Heimlich maneuver to drive out the stuck object.
-If the victim has passed out, lay them down on their back, and vigorously push the abdomen towards the diaphragm until the airway is clear again.
-Start coughing, and if it doesn’t help, perform the Heimlich maneuver on yourself.
-Place your hands as close to the abdomen as possible, higher than you normally would and perform the Heimlich maneuver.
-If the victim is less than a year old, lay them face down on your forearm, make five quick blows right between the infant’s shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
-Stand behind the child or if they’re really small, get on your knees. Clench one hand into a fist and place it between the ribs and belly button with your thumb inwards, move your elbows to the sides and press the child’s stomach.
-If the infant or child is unconscious, try laying them on their back first and try to remove the stuck objects with your fingers. If the child still isn’t breathing or if you were unable to dislodge the object from the start, begin chest compressions.
-Open the dog’s mouth with one hand on the upper jaw and the other on the lower, carefully remove the stuck object with a set of pliers. If and only if nothing else helps, administer the Heimlich maneuver.

title: Choking Infant: The Back Slap and Chest Thrust Technique, Step by Step
description:
Choking in an infant requires a completely different technique than choking in an adult or older child — and getting the head position and hand placement wrong can make the maneuver ineffective. This lesson walks through the correct response to a choking infant, step by step.

Support the infant face-down along your forearm, with the head lower than the chest and the jaw supported — this position uses gravity to help dislodge the obstruction. Deliver five firm, distinct back slaps with the heel of your hand, not gentle taps. Then perform the sandwich turn, moving the infant between your forearms while keeping the head and neck supported throughout. Finish with five chest thrusts using two fingers, positioned and delivered slower and deeper than standard infant CPR compressions.

What you'll learn in this infant choking lesson:
- Correct positioning: head lower than chest, jaw supported
- How to deliver five effective back slaps
- The sandwich turn between back slaps and chest thrusts
- Two-finger chest thrust technique for a choking infant

This lesson is part of the Basic Life Support (BLS) course for healthcare providers, based on the ILCOR Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations, as implemented in the 2020 AHA Guidelines for CPR and ECC. This is an independent training course and is not an official American Heart Association, European Resuscitation Council, or ILCOR-certified program.

transcript: As a new parent, learning CPR is very important. Thousands of babies are saved every year because someone knew CPR and started it right away. Knowing CPR can help prevent brain damage in your child if they stop breathing. CPR stands for cardiopulmonary resuscitation. CPR helps keep blood and oxygen flowing to the heart and brain when the heart stops. In this video you will learn the basics of infant CPR. Infant CPR is only for babies less than a year old. CPR for children and adults is slightly different. Anyone who cares for an infant should, and can, learn CPR. (Speaker #1) If you find your baby unresponsive or not breathing… 1. Tap the baby’s foot and shout to see if they respond. Never shake a baby. 2. If the baby does not respond, yell for help. 3. If someone comes, tell them to call 911. 4. Check for breathing. 5. If the baby is not breathing, they need CPR right away. 6. Carefully move the baby to a firm, flat surface, above ground. 7. Place two fingers in the middle of the baby’s chest, just below the nipple line. 8. Give 30 compressions by pressing straight down about 1 ½ inches. 9. Push hard and fast, at least 100 compressions per minute, and let the chest rise all the way back up after each push. 10. Next, give two breaths by putting your mouth over the baby’s mouth and nose. 11. Gently give enough breath to make the baby’s chest rise. 12. Keep alternating two breaths and 30 compressions until the baby responds or trained help arrives. If the baby is still unresponsive after two minutes of CPR and you have no help to call 911, carry the baby with you to the phone, and make the call yourself. You can continue giving compressions and breaths with the baby in a football hold. Every five days in the United States, at least one child dies from choking. When an infant is choking, quick action can be lifesaving. Continue watching to learn what to do when a child is choking. If a baby is choking but is able to cough and breathe, allow them to do so. It allows their own reflexes to clear the airway. If you know a baby is choking and they are having trouble breathing or they stop breathing, begin a sequence of five back slaps and five chest thrusts. This is what it looks like: 1. Hold the baby face down on your forearm with its head lower than its body. Make sure the baby’s head and neck are supported. 2. Give five firm slaps on the baby’s back with the heel of your hand. Deliver the slap between the baby’s shoulder blades. 3. If the object does not come out, turn the baby over onto their back. 4. Support the head and neck with your arm, and keep the baby’s head below their body. 5. Now give five chest thrusts. Use two fingers and press down in the middle of the baby’s chest just below the nipple line, like you did in CPR. 6. Repeat five back blows and five chest thrusts until a. The object is coughed up b. The baby begins to breathe, or c. The baby becomes unconscious 7. If the baby becomes unconscious, follow the steps of infant CPR that you’ve already learned 8. Each time you give breaths, look to see if the object has come out. 9. If you see an object in the mouth, take it out. Any baby that receives CPR or choking treatment should be seen by a doctor to make sure they’re all right. Thank you for watching this video. Please practice with a nurse and on a mannequin until you feel comfortable doing it on your own.

So what do you do if a kid under 8 years old goes into cardiac arrest? Ideally, you swap in a smaller set of pediatric pads or you press the pediatric setting on the device. This physically tells the machine to lower the shock energy. But most public AED kits only have adult pads and searching for alternatives wastes critical seconds. The emergency work around you use the adult pads anyway. An immediate shock is always better than delaying care for perfect equipment. But there's one strict rule when putting those oversized adult pads on a small frame, they have to be placed so their edges never touch each other. And that young child who collapsed in cardiac arrest from the very beginning, they successfully receive the life saving shock that they urgently need without any dangerous pad overlap.
