transcript: Hey, guys, it's Nurse Gwenny. Let's talk about why in PALS or pediatric Advanced Life support, they teach us, if it is a single provider, to do our chest compressions like this. Whereas if we are dual provider, we have two people on scene, we're going to use the thumb encircling technique. Also, the rate changes. If you're by yourself, you're gonna do 30 to 2, whereas if you have a partner, you're gonna do 15 to 2. So why is it any different? Well, here's why. We know that this is not as effective or not as efficient at providing adequate CPR to infants as the thumbs encircling technique. So why would they have you do it this way? Because it takes so long to transition from thumbs encircling technique to then grabbing the BVM, placing it on your kiddo appropriately, and providing those ventilations as it would to just go from a two fingers on the chest, delivering those compressions. We know that the number one cause of pediatric cardiac arrest is hypoxia, so ventilations are the priority anytime we're working on these pediatric patients. And so we don't want to waste a whole bunch of time making this transition from chest compressions to then seating the mask on there appropriately, getting your. Your airway open and position, and providing those breasts. We're gonna have a lot more lag time. So when there are two of us, I don't have to come off the chest. I count out Loud, 13, 14, 15. description:
For more information on choking first aid: https://www.massgeneralbrigham.org/en/about/newsroom/articles/choking-first-aid 

What should you do if someone is choking? Melisa W. Lai-Becker, MD, Emergency Medicine Physician at Mass General Brigham, discusses how to respond to someone choking, and how to perform the Heimlich maneuver on adults and infants. Choking symptoms include a person not being able to make a sound, holding their neck, or turning color in their face. Call for emergency help immediately and begin providing care. First, try hitting between the shoulder blades, firmly and sharply with the heel of your hand, 5 times. If that doesn’t work, begin doing the Heimlich maneuver, where you stand behind the choking person and give firm abdominal thrusts above their belly button. For infants, hold them face down with their bottoms above their heads, and hit firmly on the back 5 times. Keep alternating back blows and the Heimlich maneuver until medical help arrives. Choking can happen anywhere and anytime, but by staying calm and providing care, you can help save a life.

title: 6e: AED for Children (2026)
description:
The fifth lesson in chapter six discusses AED use in children. There are step-by-step directions for use provided. It is important to follow the prompts on the AED. 

An AED can deliver a pediatric shock to restart the heart. The steps for using an AED in children are the same as those in adults. Always check the AED when it arrives on the scene. If the child is younger than eight years, then use pediatric pads. If pediatric pads are not available, standard, that is adult pads, may be used. If you are using standard pads, make sure that the pads do not overlap each other. If needed, put one of the pads on the child’s back.

Some AEDs have a switch that can be set to deliver a pediatric shock. If available, turn this switch on when using AED for children younger than eight years. If the AED cannot deliver a pediatric shock, an adult shock should be given. Be sure to start CPR.

To use an AED on a child, first, turn the power on.
Expose the child’s chest. Then, apply the pads. Ensure that the pads do not touch.
Connect the pads.
Clear the child so no one is touching the child. Analyze the rhythm.
Follow the prompts: Shock Advised, No Shock Advised, Check Connection, etc. Resume CPR with compressions.

transcript: What to do if your baby is choking. I'm Doctor Yoshi, board certified pediatrician. I've gotten a ton of messages asking for a demonstration of what to do if your baby is choking, so here are the steps. First, recognize the signs. If a baby is choking, they might not be able to cry or cough. They might have difficulty breathing, and their skin might turn blue, especially around the lips and face. If you see these signs, act quickly but calmly. First, yell for help and have somebody call emergency services. If you are alone and have your phone accessible, call emergency services, put it on speaker, and quickly move to the next step. Next, for babies under one, support their head and their jaw with your hand. Place them on your forearm, facing down, and make sure that their head is below their chest. Give up to five firm back blows between the baby's shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. If the object isn't dislodged, turn the baby over onto their back, supporting them with your arm. Make sure their head is still below their chest, and perform five chest thrusts using two fingers in the center of their chest.

Here is what you need to do – fast and step by step: 🚨 Emergency situation – stay calm and act! ⸻ 🟢 1 If the baby is still coughing • 👶 Do not interfere • 💨 Coughing is good → the baby is trying to clear the airway • 👀 Only observe ⸻ 🔴 2 If the baby is NOT breathing properly / no effective cough 👇 Step 1: Back blows • 👶 Place the baby face down on your forearm (head lower than the body) • ✋ Support the head at the lower jaw (do not press the soft throat!) • 💥 Give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades ⸻ 👇 Step 2: Chest thrusts • 👶 Turn the baby face up, still keeping the head low • ✌️ Use two fingers on the breastbone (as in CPR) • 💥 Give 5 quick chest thrusts ⸻ 🔁 3 Repeat • 🔄 Repeat steps 1 and 2 as long as the baby is choking ⸻ ⚠️ 4 If the baby becomes unresponsive • 📞 Call emergency services for your country • 💨 Start with 5 initial breaths  • 💓 Then start CPR: 30 compressions + 2 breaths ⸻ 💓 CPR – Babies (0–12 months) • 👤 1 rescuer: 30 compressions + 2 breaths • 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 2 rescuers: 15 compressions + 2 breaths ⸻ 🧒 CPR – Children (about 1 year to puberty) • 👤 1 rescuer: 30 : 2 • 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 2 rescuers: 15 : 2 ⸻ 👨 CPR – Adults • 👤 + 🧑‍🤝‍🧑 always 30 : 2 (no change with 2 rescuers) ⸻ ❗ Important • 🚫 Never use abdominal thrusts on babies • 🚫 Never put fingers blindly into the mouth (only remove the object if you can clearly see it)

If a child (1–12 years) is unresponsive and not breathing normally, every second counts. Early CPR and rapid defibrillation give them the best possible chance of survival.

Call 999 immediately, start CPR without delay, and begin with rescue breaths if the collapse is likely breathing-related. Keep compressions steady and effective, and use an AED as soon as it arrives — paediatric mode if available, but never delay a shock.

title: Neonatal Resuscitation | TOACS & OSCE Station
description:
Neonatal resuscitation, also known as newborn resuscitation, is an emergency procedure focused on supporting approximately 10% of newborn children who do not readily begin breathing putting them at risk of irreversible organ injury and death. During Neonatal Resuscitation, make sure that the environment is neat, clean and safe. Baby should be received in dry, warm wrapping sheet. If baby doesn’t start breathing with drying, then stimulate the back of the baby and the sole. If baby doesn’t start breathing with drying, start suctioning of mouth and then Nose. Give 5 rescue breaths with Ambu Bag in neutral position (Head down, chin lift). After initial 5 rescue breaths, assess the baby for color and breathing.  If baby is still not breathing check the heart rate with stethoscope. If still not breathing. Give adrenaline 0.2 ml / kg (with the concentration of 1 in 10,000). If no response in 20 minutes we can stop resuscitation process.

🚨 DO NOT DO CPR if the person is awake, conscious or responsive  🚨 For a 1-year-old child, use the heel of 1 hand for chest compressions. 🚨 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths  🚨 Roll to the side only for vomiting. Drowning victims frequently vomit or regurgitate water and stomach contents. Roll them onto their side to prevent choking, and gently clear their mouth before rolling them onto their back again. What Happens If You Perform CPR on a Conscious Person 1. Extreme Physical Injury and PainChest compressions require significant force. If performed on someone whose heart is already pumping, they will experience severe pain. The heavy pressure can easily result in:Fractured or broken ribsA broken sternum (breastbone)Collapsed or punctured lungsI nternal bleeding or damaged organs (like the liver or spleen) 2. Disrupted Heart RhythmCompressing a beating heart can force it out of its normal rhythm. This can trigger life-threatening arrhythmias (such as ventricular fibrillation), which could cause the heart to actually stop pumping effectively. 3. Psychological TraumaExperiencing forceful, unnecessary chest compressions and rescue breaths while awake is a deeply terrifying and traumatic event. It can lead to long-term severe psychological distress and post-traumatic stress. 4. Legal ConsequencesGood Samaritan laws and "implied consent" only protect rescuers when the victim is unconscious, unresponsive, or unable to give consent. Performing CPR on a conscious, competent person who has not consented to the treatment can result in civil or criminal charges for assault and battery.#greenscreen #greenscreenvideo

title: PEDIATRIC CPR Explained Simply
description:

Get my EKG/12-Lead EKG Masterclass: https://www.ekgforems.com

Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) according to the American Heart Association (AHA) involves specific steps tailored to infants and children up to puberty. The process begins with ensuring the scene is safe for both the rescuer and the patient. Once safety is confirmed, check the child’s responsiveness by gently tapping and shouting. For infants, you should tap the bottom of the foot. If there is no response, activate the emergency response system. If you are alone with a child or infant and there is no response, perform CPR for 2 minutes before leaving to call emergency services. If another person is present, have them call emergency services immediately.

Next, open the airway using the head-tilt-chin-lift technique. Be careful with the amount of tilt, especially in infants. Check for breathing and a pulse for no more than 10 seconds. For infants, check the brachial pulse, and for children, check the carotid or femoral pulse. 

For chest compressions in infants (under 1 year), use two fingers in the center of the chest, just below the nipple line, pressing to a depth of at least 1.5 inches (4 cm) at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute. For children (1 year to puberty), use one or two hands (depending on the size of the child) on the lower half of the breastbone, pressing to a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm), but not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm), at the same rate of 100-120 compressions per minute.

After compressions, provide rescue breaths. For both infants and children, give 2 breaths after every 30 compressions (or 15:2 if two rescuers are present). Each breath should last about 1 second and make the chest rise visibly. Use an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) as soon as it is available. For infants and children under 8 years, use pediatric pads if available. If not, use adult pads, placing them so they do not touch each other. Follow the AED prompts and resume CPR immediately after each shock, continuing until the child shows signs of life or emergency medical personnel take over.

Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths (or 15:2 if two rescuers are present) until the child shows signs of life, an AED is ready to use, or professional help arrives. These steps ensure that CPR provided to pediatric patients follows the AHA's guidelines for optimal outcomes.

transcript: Knowing how to perform CPR on a baby or child can save lives. Let's walk through the steps. I'm Doctor Yoshi, board certified pediatrician. First, check for responsiveness, then check for breathing. This should take 10 seconds or less. If the baby is non responsive and not breathing or gasping for air, shout for help and call emergency services. If you're alone and have access to your phone, call emergency services. Put your phone on speaker and quickly move to the next step. Next, place the baby on their back on a firm, flat surface with their head and neck in line and start CPR. For babies under one, place two fingers at the center of their chest, just below the nipple line. Or wrap your arms around the baby and place your two thumbs in the same location on the chest. For those 1 and older, interlace your hands and place them in the center of the chest. For those under one, push down one and a/2 inches or 4 centimeters, and for those one and up, push down 2 inches or 5 centimeters. Allow the chest to rise. Between compressions, perform 30 compressions at a rate of 100 to 1 20 per minute. Compress to the song staying alive to stay on beat. After 30 compressions, give two rescue breaths. Cover the nose and mouth with your mouth, creating a seal. If you can't cover the whole nose and mouth, pinch the nose and cover the mouth. Make sure the Head is in the neutral position for babies and slightly tilted back for kids. To open the airway, give gentle breaths, just enough to make the chest rise and fall. Continue the cycle of 30 compressions and two rescue breaths until help arrives or the child starts breathing. If you've performed five cycles and haven't called emergency services, stop to call and get an AED if accessible, then continue. Practice these steps often and consider taking a certified CPR course. Your preparedness can make all the difference in an emergency. Share this video to spread awareness.

Choking is a life-threatening situation and happens when the casualty's airway suddenly gets blocked so they cannot breathe normally. Their airway can be partly or fully blocked. Usually, choking in small children is caused by a small foreign object whereas in adults it is most commonly food. If the blockage of the airway is mild, the casualty should be able to clear it by coughing. transcript: In my previous video we spoke about choking in children. Today I'm going to take you through the techniques of how you give back blows, chest thrust, abdominal thrust and mouth motorisation. If your child is choking, has ineffective cough, however they are conscious, you need to deliver back blows. So place your child facing downwards on your lap, support their head. You deliver five blows in between their shoulder blades. Every time you do this, check their mouth to see if the foreign body has come out. You are able to see it and grasp and remove it out if you can see it. If not, you need to now continue to give chest thrust. For the chest thrust, now lay your baby facing upwards with your two fingers, place them on the lower part of their chest and deliver five chest thrust by compressing around 2 to 3 cm. For children more than 1 year of age, you can replace the chest thrust with abdominal thrust. You can either stand behind or kneel behind the child. Wrap your arms around the waist with your fist, closed fist with the thumb facing upwards, place it on their abdomen just above their navel and below their breastbone. Encircle the other hand onto this wrist so that it can give you support and deliver quick thrusts which are upward and inward. Five times. You need to repeat these cycles of back blows, chest thrust or abdominal thrust one after the other. Until the object is expelled out, until your child is conscious. If your child is unconscious, however, you need to do mouth to mouth resuscitation. For the mouth to mouth resuscitation, place the baby on a firm surface, tilt the head to open the airway, establish that there is no breathing. So you look for the breathing movements of the chest. You listen if there are any breathing sounds that you can hear and you feel for the gush of air with any breath. If there's nothing suggestive of breathing, you now seal your lips to the mouth and nose of the baby and breathe steadily for around 1 second. These are called rescue breaths. Give five such rescue breaths to your baby. Soon after this, now you have to deliver chest compressions using your two fingers on the lower part of the chest. You compress 30 times at the depth of 2 to 3 cm. After every 30 compressions, you need to give two rescue breaths. Continue this cycle continuously until you get help. These techniques are extremely important and life-saving measures. Please feel free to reach out to me if you have any further questions or clarifications.

title: Using An AED On A Child
description:
---

👶 How to Use an AED on a Child | CPR & Defibrillator Guide
Early defibrillation can save a child’s life during sudden cardiac arrest.

🚨 Steps to Follow:
✓ Ensure the area is safe
✓ Check for response – tap and shout
✓ If not breathing normally, call 999 or 112 and get an AED
✓ Give 5 rescue breaths, then 30 chest compressions
✓ Continue with 30 compressions and 2 breaths until the AED arrives

⚡ Using the AED:
✓ Turn it on and follow voice prompts
✓ Use child mode or paediatric pads if available
✓ If not, use adult pads – one on the chest, one on the back
✓ Do not touch the child while the AED analyses the heart
✓ If shock advised, make sure no one is touching the child and press the shock button (or the AED will deliver the shock automatically if it's a fully automatic model)

❤️ After the Shock:
✓ Resume CPR immediately
✓ Follow the AED instructions
✓ Only stop if the child starts breathing, help arrives, or you're told to stop

✅ AEDs are safe, simple and require no training. Act fast. Stay calm. Save a life.

description:
The Neonatal Life Support Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations states that chest compressions be performed preferably with the 2-thumb encircling technique. The aim of this study was to compare the hemodynamic effects of four different finger positions during chest compressions in a piglet model of neonatal asphyxia. Methods: Seven asphyxiated post-transitional piglets were randomized to chest compressions with 2-thumb-, 2-finger-, knocking-fingers-, and over-the-head 2-thumb-techniques for one minute at each technique. Chest compressions superimposed with sustained inflations were performed manually. 
Conclusion: The 2-thumb-technique and the over-the-head 2-thumb-technique resulted in improved slope rises of carotid blood flow and dp/dtmin during chest compression.

transcript: Properly handling infant choking incidents. Choking is a common and dangerous condition for infants. Parents should watch this video to learn how to handle it promptly. There are four signs for parents to recognize if their child is choking. While feeding suddenly, the baby becomes silent, stiffens, and turns blue, or when lying down after eating, the baby suddenly chokes, turns blue, and faints. The child may panic, stiffen, or become limp. Milk may overflow from the baby's nose and mouth without timely first aid, the child may stop breathing, and their heart may stop. When a child is choking, parents should lay them on their side, tilt their hand flat, and pat between the baby's shoulder blades to let the milk in the baby's mouth flow out. If the child doesn't recover, parents should quickly lay the child face down, pat continuously between the child's shoulder blades. After padding, gently turn the child over to see if they can breathe on their own and if their skin is rosier. Once the child has recovered, parents should still take them to the nearest medical center for further observation.

transcript: [CHIMING] CPR is a life-saving action that can get oxygen and blood to the brain in an emergency. Getting trained in CPR is the best way to be prepared, but knowing the basics can help save a life. If a baby doesn't seem to be breathing, shout and tap the bottom of the feet and see if there's any response. Lay the baby face up on a flat, firm surface. Kneel or stand to one side. You may be taught to check for breathing by seeing if the chest is moving, but don't spend more than 10 seconds doing this. Next, shout for help. Have someone call 911 and get an AED, Automated External Defibrillator, if possible, while you start CPR. If you're alone and have a phone, call 911 and then begin CPR. Leave the phone on speaker. title: Paediatric Basic Life Support - 2021 key points from the UK Resus
description:
The 2021 UK Resuscitation Council guidelines have added a few key points about Paediatric basic life support.  In the paediatric basic life support sequence, rescuers should perform an assessment for signs of life, like circulation, simultaneously with breathing assessment and during the delivery of rescue breaths.  If there are no signs of life, chest compressions should be started immediately after rescue breaths have been delivered.

There is an emphasis on rescuers using mobile phones with speaker function to facilitate bystander access to dispatcher guided cardiopulmonary resuscitation known as CPR and to summon emergency medical services (EMS) without leaving the child or infant.

In certain situations, such as when the child or infant is breathing spontaneously but requires airway management or when the child has a traumatic injury, the recovery position is not recommended. In these circumstances:

Keep the patient flat, maintain an open airway by either continued head tilt and chin lift or jaw thrust.

For trauma victims, leave the child or infant lying flat and open and maintain the airway using a jaw thrust, taking care to avoid spinal movement.

High-quality CPR is emphasised in the guidelines which are obtained by:

A chest compression depth is at least one third the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest, or by 4 cm for the infant and 5 cm for the child.

The chest compression pauses are minimised so that 80% or more of the CPR cycle is comprised of chest compressions chest at a  rate of 100 to 120 per min. And finally by allowing full recoil of the chest after each chest compression.

title: This is one of the most important differences between pediatric and adult resuscitation. Pediatric bradycardia is frequently caused by **hypoxemia and respiratory failure**. That's why the initial priorities include: • Opening the airway • Providing oxygen • Supporting effective ventilation But what if the heart rate remains **below 60 beats per minute** and the child still has signs of cardiopulmonary compromise? That's when PALS directs you to begin **chest compressions, even when a pulse is still present.** Here's the physiology behind it: **Cardiac Output = Heart Rate × Stroke Volume** Infants, especially neonates and young infants, have a more limited ability to increase stroke volume compared with adults. That makes their cardiac output much more dependent on heart rate. So when the heart rate becomes severely slow, cardiac output can fall quickly. And here's the important part: A palpable pulse does NOT automatically mean perfusion is adequate. A child may still have a pulse but not have enough cardiac output to maintain adequate: • Coronary perfusion • Cerebral perfusion • End organ oxygen delivery But don't reduce this to: Heart rate below 60 = CPR. Three things matter: 1. The heart rate is below 60 beats per minute 2. Cardiopulmonary compromise is present 3. The bradycardia persists **despite effective ventilation with oxygen** And that last part matters. If oxygenation and ventilation are not effective, correcting the respiratory problem is critical because **hypoxemia may be what is driving the bradycardia in the first place.** Another high yield distinction: Atropine is NOT the universal first medication for pediatric bradycardia. Atropine is considered when increased vagal tone or primary AV block is suspected. The treatment pathway depends on the cause. The monitor tells you the rate. Perfusion tells you whether that rate is producing enough cardiac output. title: What to Do If a Baby Is Choking If an infant under 1 year is choking, do not do the Heimlich. The correct first aid is: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts, and repeat. Hold the baby face-down on your forearm, with the head lower than the chest, and give 5 back blows between the shoulder blades. Then turn the baby face-up, keep the head lower than the chest, and give 5 chest thrusts using two fingers in the center of the chest, just below the nipple line. Repeat 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out or the baby can breathe or cry. If the baby becomes unresponsive, call emergency services and begin CPR. #ParentingTips #ParentingAdvice #Pediatrician #PediatricianTips #BabySafety

This lecture provides a detailed analysis of the 2025 American Heart Association (AHA) Guideline Updates for Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS), Basic Life Support (BLS) for Infants and Children, and Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP). We review the significant changes, including drug administration timing, airway management techniques, and key shifts in neonatal care like delayed cord clamping. It is a critical guide for healthcare professionals looking to understand the nuanced updates in resuscitation protocols for the youngest patients.

What You'll Learn Section
The recommendation for early epinephrine administration in pediatric non-shockable rhythms (PEA and asystole).

New physiological monitoring targets during pediatric CPR, including diastolic blood pressure (hospital setting).

Updated guidance for managing pediatric FBAO (foreign body airway obstruction), consistent across all age groups.

The controversial addition of antiarrhythmic agents (Procainamide, Amiodarone, Sotalol) for adenosine-refractory pediatric SVT.

Key changes in umbilical cord management, including deferred clamping for 60 seconds and cord milking for non-vigorous term newborns.

Updated targets for neonatal ventilation rates (30-60 breaths/min) and the initial use of LMA/Video Laryngoscopy.

The shift to using 100% oxygen during neonatal chest compressions, regardless of prior saturation.

The unchanged nature of most major PALS and NRP algorithms, highlighting ambiguous time frames that remain for pulse checks/ventilation.
